stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Pteropods, often called sea butterflies, are snails that have abandoned the seafloor. Over millions of years, the muscular foot that a garden snail uses to creep has evolved in pteropods into two thin flaps, which the animals beat to "fly" through open water. Many species are smaller than a lentil. Some feed by releasing a web of mucus several times their body width and then reeling it in along with the plankton caught in it. Pteropods are in turn a major food source for fish such as salmon and mackerel.
choices: To explain how pteropods use mucus webs to capture plankton
To argue that pteropods deserve more study from marine scientists
To describe a group of tiny snails that live in open water
To show that pteropods move in much the same way garden snails do
explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. Each one gives a fact about pteropods: how they swim, how small they are, how they feed and what eats them. Together they profile a group of small snails that live in open water. The text only informs, so the neutral verb "describe" fits, and the choice covers the whole passage rather than one detail.

A.why: You picked a detail that really is in the text. The mucus web appears in only one sentence, so it is too narrow to be the purpose of a passage that also covers the animals' swimming, size and place in the food web.

B.why: You chose a verb that is too strong. The text never gives an opinion or says pteropods need more research. It only presents facts, so "argue" claims more than the passage does.

D.why: You reversed the comparison the text makes. The passage says the foot a garden snail uses to creep has evolved in pteropods into flaps for swimming. That is a difference between the two animals, not a similarity.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Mapmaker Lucia Ferrand spent the 1950s producing maps of the Alpine valleys around her hometown, and hikers still seek them out today. Rather than shading mountains in uniform gray, Ferrand blended soft greens, browns, and violets so that slopes facing the morning sun appeared lighter than those in shadow. She also drew every footpath by hand after walking it herself, often marking springs and shelters that official surveys had missed. Her sheets were printed in small runs by a local press and now sell for many times their original price.
choices: To describe the methods and lasting appeal of one mapmaker's work
To explain how Ferrand chose the colors she used for her slopes
To argue that official surveys of the Alps were poorly made
To show that Ferrand's maps were printed in large numbers
explanation: Every sentence is about Ferrand's maps: when she made them, how she colored the slopes, how she drew the paths, and why the maps are still valued. Together they profile one mapmaker's techniques and her work's lasting appeal. The text is neutral, so "describe" is the right verb, and the choice covers the whole passage.

B.why: You picked a true detail instead of the purpose. The colors appear in one sentence, and the passage goes on to cover her footpaths and the maps' value today, so this choice is too narrow.

C.why: You let one passing remark become the point. The text says only that Ferrand marked some springs and shelters that official surveys had missed. It never criticizes those surveys or argues that they were badly made.

D.why: You misread the facts. The passage says the maps were printed "in small runs," which is the opposite of large numbers. Even if that detail were right, it would be too narrow to be the main purpose.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Economist Teodora Vance spent two decades studying seasonal farmworkers in California's Central Valley. Rather than relying on government surveys, she rode buses with work crews before dawn and wrote down what each worker earned that day. Her handwritten ledgers, now held at a university library, are among the most detailed wage records from the period. Researchers still use them to trace how pay changed from one harvest season to the next.
choices: To describe an economist's research method and the lasting use of the records it produced
To explain why government surveys of farmworkers' wages were unreliable during that period
To note where a collection of handwritten wage ledgers is currently being kept
To argue that economists should give more recognition to Vance's research on wages
explanation: Every sentence is about Vance's work. It covers how she gathered data, what her ledgers contain, and how researchers still use them. A covers the whole text with a neutral verb ('describe'), which fits a passage that only informs.

B.why: The text says Vance didn't rely on government surveys, but it never says those surveys were unreliable. You read a criticism into a passage that doesn't make one.

C.why: The ledgers really are held at a university library, but that is one detail in one sentence. You picked a true detail instead of the purpose of the whole text.

D.why: 'Argue' needs an explicit opinion, and the text gives none. It informs you about Vance's work without saying she deserves more recognition.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: The Ridgeline Network is a group of 140 low-cost seismometers installed in schools across a mountainous region. Each device, roughly the size of a shoebox, records ground motion and sends its data to a central server every second. Students check the readings during science classes, and seismologists use the same data to locate small earthquakes that larger, more widely spaced stations can miss.
choices: To present the features of a seismometer network and the ways its data are used
To compare the accuracy of low-cost seismometers with that of larger stations
To point out that each seismometer in a network is about the size of a shoebox
To argue that every school should install a seismometer for its own students
explanation: The text says what the Ridgeline Network is, how its devices work, and who uses the data: students and seismologists. A is the only choice broad enough to cover all of that, and its neutral verb matches the informative tone.

B.why: The text says the network catches small quakes that widely spaced stations miss, but it never compares the instruments' accuracy. You added a comparison the text doesn't make.

C.why: The shoebox size is in the text, but it is a single detail. You chose one true fact instead of the purpose that ties every sentence together.

D.why: The text describes a network that already exists and never recommends anything. 'Argue that every school should' is too strong for a passage that only informs.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: In the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, a fallen tree can stay useful for centuries. As the trunk slowly decays, its soft, moist wood becomes a seedbed for hemlock and spruce seedlings, which struggle to take root on the crowded forest floor. Fungi, insects, and salamanders also shelter inside these "nurse logs," which support new life long after the original tree has died.
choices: To describe how fallen trees in certain forests go on supporting other living things
To explain why hemlock and spruce seedlings rarely survive on the forest floor
To argue that fallen trees should be left in place rather than cleared from forests
To show that nurse logs support new growth only while the original tree is alive
explanation: Every sentence is about what a fallen tree does for other organisms: seedlings, fungi, insects, and salamanders. A states that shared idea with a neutral verb.

B.why: The text mentions that seedlings struggle on the forest floor, but only to explain why nurse logs matter. You treated a supporting detail as the purpose of the whole text.

C.why: The text never says what forest managers should do. 'Argue' needs a stated opinion, and this passage only describes.

D.why: The text says nurse logs support new life 'long after the original tree has died.' This choice reverses that.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Engineer Lucinda Ferrante designed the Marlow Footbridge, which opened in 1974 across a narrow river gorge. Instead of hanging the deck from steel cables, she joined a series of precast concrete segments with tensioned rods, a method that let crews build the bridge without scaffolding in the gorge below. The footbridge still carries hikers today, and several later bridges in the region copied its design.
choices: To describe a footbridge's unusual design and the influence that design has had
To explain why scaffolding could not be put up in a narrow river gorge
To argue that concrete is a better material for bridges than steel cables
To suggest that the footbridge was closed once later bridges replaced it
explanation: The text introduces the Marlow Footbridge, explains its unusual construction, and ends with its legacy: it is still in use and was copied by later bridges. A covers both parts with a neutral verb.

B.why: Building without scaffolding is one benefit of Ferrante's method, and the text never explains why scaffolding was impossible. You fixed on a single detail instead of the purpose of the whole text.

C.why: The text says Ferrante used concrete instead of cables, not that concrete is better in general. 'Argue' is too strong for a passage that only informs.

D.why: The text says the footbridge 'still carries hikers today.' Later bridges copied its design. They did not replace it.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: The Ashgrove sample books, kept by a small cotton-printing works in northern England from 1820 to 1860, hold more than 9,000 swatches of printed fabric. Beside each swatch, clerks wrote the dye recipe, the customer's name, and the price per yard. Because so few printed cottons from that period survive as clothing, textile historians rely on the books to learn which colors and patterns ordinary buyers chose.
choices: To introduce a collection of fabric samples and explain why historians value it
To point out that clerks recorded a customer's name beside each fabric swatch
To argue that surviving clothing is a misleading source for textile historians
To show that the printing works produced only a few patterns on its cotton
explanation: The text says what the Ashgrove sample books are, what they record, and why historians rely on them. A covers both what the collection is and why it matters, and it uses a neutral verb.

B.why: The clerks did record customers' names, but that is one item in a list. You picked a true detail instead of the purpose of the whole text.

C.why: The text says little clothing survives. It never says that clothing is misleading. You turned a statement about scarcity into a criticism the text doesn't make.

D.why: The books hold more than 9,000 swatches. That is the opposite of 'only a few patterns.'
